citation.source: COMPUTED from this repo's OWN real, cited data, not an external assumption — added 2026-08-16 after critically reviewing a user-supplied external report whose own assumed composition (70/6/12/11/1% water/protein/carb/fat/ash) had no derivation or bibliography. Composition: potato.json (water_g=79, carbohydrate_g=17) + egg.json (water_g=76, protein_g=13, fat_g=11, carbohydrate_g=1.1), weighted 3:1 potato:egg by mass (a commonly-cited traditional ratio — convergent Spanish recipe sources converge on roughly 1kg potato to ~6 large eggs, ~350g, close to 3:1) — giving water=78.25, carbohydrate=13.03, protein=3.25, fat=2.75 per 100g (97.3% tracked). specificHeatJPerKgK (3713 J/(kg*K)) is REAL Choi-Okos (1986), same method and same already-verified component equations potato.json/onion.json/egg.json use: carbohydrate/protein/fat component cp evaluated at the same 50C reference (1632/2065/2046 J/(kg*K) respectively — the carbohydrate figure exactly reproduces potato.json's own already-computed 1632, a real cross-check, not a coincidence, since it's the identical equation/reference temperature), water component reuses water.json's own already-cited 4186 J/(kg*K) rather than re-deriving it (Choi-Okos gives 4185.3 at 50C — a 0.02% difference, corroborating 4186 rather than contradicting it). densityKgPerM3/thermalConductivityWPerMK are a simple mass-weighted interpolation of potato.json's (1080, 0.5) and egg.json's (1030, 0.34) own already-cited values by the same 3:1 ratio, NOT independently measured or Choi-Okos-computed — same 'recalled/interpolated as typical, not independently re-derived' caveat those two source fields already carry.
citation.note: The 3:1 potato:egg mass ratio is a real, commonly-cited but genuinely variable home-recipe proportion (real recipes range from roughly 2:1 to 4:1) — not a fixed constant, a representative choice. Oil is deliberately NOT included as a separate weighted component: real published oil-absorption data exists for high-temperature deep/par-frying (23-28% at 160-180C, a genuinely different scope than tortilla-de-patatas.json's own established low-heat, long-duration confit-style technique for potato), and no citable oil-absorption figure was found that scope-matches THIS technique specifically — omitted rather than borrowing a mismatched number, the same scope-mismatch discipline garlic_peel.json's/onion_peel.json's yield-fraction citations already apply. This likely means the real fat content is somewhat higher than the 2.75g/100g stated here — a real, named, probably-conservative underestimate, not a claim of completeness.

citation.source: DERIVED, not directly cited: a commonly-cited home tortilla pan size (24cm/9-10in) combined with a real mass (1kg potato + 350g egg, the same 3:1 ratio used for composition above) and this entity's own just-computed density (1068 kg/m3) gives a real, computed total thickness of ~2.8cm for a 24cm-diameter pan — see LEARNINGS_ENGINE.md 2026-08-16 for the full derivation. typicalDiameterCm records the PAN size assumption (a real, commonly-cited range across consumer recipe sources), not a measured tortilla property directly — src/heat-penetration.ts's slab model instead needs the resulting THICKNESS, computed on demand from mass/density/pan-area rather than stored as a second, potentially-inconsistent field here.
citation.note: A real derivation from this entity's own already-cited density and a commonly-cited pan size, not an independently measured or peer-reviewed geometric fact — flagged at the same tier as the composition/mass-ratio assumptions it depends on.

metadata.notes: The first entity in this repo to actually populate structure.composite/components (potato + egg) — that field existed, unused, since ingredient.ts's first draft; see data/actions/combine.json. Result of COMBINE-ing a fried-potato instance with a beaten-egg instance (see data/actions/combine.json's requiredTargetCapability/requiredSecondaryCapability). possibleTags 'flipped' rather than a state: flipping doesn't change WHAT the mixture is (still 'fried' — it's mid-cook, on its second side), matching SALT's addsTag precedent, not a new transformedState.
metadata.restNote: isRestable + REST (data/actions/rest.json), added 2026-08-16 in direct response to a user's real-world correction: this recipe's own combine-then-immediately-fry sequence was missing a real, named technique step. Real tortilla de patatas recipes commonly instruct resting the just-combined mixture 5-20 minutes before it goes back in the pan — see REFERENCES.md for the convergent consumer-recipe sources. Two genuinely different real effects are commonly cited for why, both worth naming even though neither is causally modeled here (informational-only tag, same depth limit as every other technique fact in this vocabulary): (1) the potato ABSORBS some of the raw egg and its flavor during the rest; (2) the potato's own RESIDUAL HEAT (untracked by this engine — see rawStateHonestyNote below) partially cooks/coagulates the egg at contact surfaces before any pan heat is applied, which is genuinely part of what gives a well-made tortilla its characteristic creamy, custardy set rather than a uniformly rubbery one.
metadata.rawStateHonestyNote: A real, named simplification, not an oversight: this entity is spawned in state 'raw' the instant COMBINE fires (engine.ts always uses combinedEntity.possibleStates[0] for a freshly-combined instance), even though — per restNote above — the egg component has typically already begun cooking a little from contact with still-hot potato by the time a human would actually look at it. This engine has NO instance-level temperature field at all (src/engine.ts's Instance is just {entityId, state, tags} — see LEARNINGS_ENGINE.md 2026-08-16), so there is no way to track 'how hot is this potato, and how much did that pre-cook the egg' without a much larger change (a real per-instance thermal model, deliberately scoped OUT of this fix — see that same LEARNINGS_ENGINE.md entry for the considered, rejected deeper alternative). REST's addsTag: 'rested' records that the wait happened; it does not, and currently cannot, adjust 'raw' to reflect the real partial cooking that already occurred by that point.
metadata.knownGap: FRY applied twice (once before FLIP, once after) both times just sets the fixed state 'fried' — this schema has no way to distinguish 'one side fried' from 'both sides fried, fully cooked', since ActionOutputsSchema.transformedState is always a fixed target regardless of the instance's current state. Left honest rather than invented new states ('fried_one_side'/'fried_both_sides') that FRY's shared, fixed-output shape can't actually support without breaking every other FRY user — same category of limitation as fry.json's doneness parameter.
metadata.flipPhysicsNote: PARTIALLY closed 2026-08-16 — see scripts/tortilla-flip-physics-as-a-robot.ts and LEARNINGS_ENGINE.md's own entry for the full reasoning, prompted directly by a user question ('is the same logic involved as agitating potato pieces') and a critical review of a user-supplied external report that got the underlying physics WRONG (it modeled a mid-cook flip as equivalent to simultaneous double-sided heating for the WHOLE duration — the physics of fully-submerged frying, not of a sequential flip). What IS real and computed, reusing heat-penetration.ts's EXISTING slab-conduction model with zero code changes (this entity's own thermophysical block above is what was actually missing): a real, honest BRACKET, not a false-precision single number. A flip-once tortilla's true center-doneness time is bounded: t_symmetric (heatedFaces:2, an idealized lower bound — both faces heated from t=0, physically impossible for an actual flip) <= t_actual_with_one_flip <= t_singleSided (heatedFaces:1, an honest upper bound — never flipping at all). Both bounds are real, computed numbers; the exact middle value for 'flipped exactly once, halfway through' is NOT computed here — that needs the actual spatial temperature profile at the flip moment as a non-uniform initial condition for stage two, which the one-term approximation this repo uses does not expose (only the CENTER temperature, via centerTempCAfterSeconds) — a real, further, named gap, not silently implied closed by the bracket.
metadata.haccpGapFound2026-08-12: criticalControlPointsByAction was MISSING entirely until asked whether tortilla de Betanzos — a real regional style defined by an intentionally liquid, barely-set interior — was makeable. Same class of bug as handmade-alioli-egg-yolk.json's original zero-enforcement gap: this entity is built from egg (COMBINE's secondary instance) and FRIED for a duration a real recipe could set arbitrarily short, with no safety check at all until this fix. Reuses egg_cooking.json (same organism, same risk, same reasoning egg_cracked.json already uses for FRY/SCRAMBLE) rather than inventing a new CCP — the risk is a fact about egg being present in the mixture, not about which composite entity it ended up in.
metadata.failureStateNote: 'burned'/'overcooked' added 2026-08-16 (TICKET 5, PAPER_NOTES_2608.04768.md) — see potato.json's identically-named note for the full reasoning this mirrors (no detection mechanism, reachable only as an authored fact). A tortilla left in the pan too long or on too-high heat burning on the outside before the (already slow-to-set, per the Betanzos style above) interior finishes is a real, commonly-experienced home-cooking failure, not a hypothetical. 'burned' is unconditionally terminal (forbids every other state including 'overcooked'). 'overcooked' forbids reverting to 'raw'/'fried' but, matching potato.json's/egg.json's identical entries, leaves the transition to 'burned' itself open (a real further progression) — so `isTerminalState(tortilla_mixture, "overcooked")` correctly computes `false`. Either way, neither has a real rescue the way potato's overcooked-then-mashed path does; it's the finished composite dish, not an intermediate ingredient with further processing options. Relates to, but does not close, this file's own pre-existing knownGap above (no way to distinguish 'one side fried' from 'both sides fried') — burned/overcooked are additional TERMINAL outcomes layered onto that same fixed-output limitation, not a fix for it.
